common_mistakes: Dropping root vegetables into already-boiling water, which cooks the outside first, leaves the center uneven and makes pieces crumble.
Trusting pre-boiled bamboo shoots as they are, without the second boil that removes the bran-like smell.
Giving dried goods a quick rinse instead of a full two-stage soak, leaving odor and grit behind.
Shelling peas or cutting everything hours ahead, when some prep is deliberately saved for the last moment.
Grilling miso-marinated fish with the marinade still on it: the miso scorches on the surface long before the center is cooked, so pros wipe it clean first.
Rinsing blanched bean sprouts under water to cool them, which washes off the salt and leaves the finished dish diluted.
Trusting your eyes for fish bones instead of your fingertips, and serving fillets with pin bones still in them.
core_principles: Remove off-flavors at the source instead of masking them later: blanching, parboiling and discarding the water take away bitterness, blood and bran-like smells.
Dense vegetables start in cold water so the heat reaches the center evenly and the pieces keep their shape.
Manage water deliberately: draw it out with salt, wipe it off, or soak it back in, depending on what the ingredient needs.
Prep decides penetration: parboiled or pierced ingredients absorb seasoning to the core in far less time.
Timing is part of prep: some things, like shelling peas, are done at the very last moment on purpose.
Break fibers on purpose: smashing, pounding and piercing open paths for seasoning in vegetables just as they do in meat.

hook_questions: Why do Japanese chefs boil fish for ten seconds before they even start cooking it?
What is the one pot of water Japanese home cooks always throw away?
Why does the real cooking in Japan happen before the stove is turned on?
Why do Japanese chefs blanch greens in water that never boils?
How do you know konnyaku is ready? It starts to sing.
key_facts: Shimofuri blanching: fish is passed briefly through boiling water until the surface just changes color, then moved to cold water and washed, removing the blood and fat that cause fishy odors and keeping the simmering liquid clear.

Root vegetables such as taro, daikon and burdock are always parboiled starting from cold water; in chikuzenni they simmer about 5 minutes after the boil so they cook evenly without crumbling and absorb flavor far better.
Even store-bought pre-boiled bamboo shoots are boiled again from cold water and the water discarded, to remove the bran-like smell so the dashi flavor can enter purely.
Konnyaku and shirataki are parboiled from cold water for about 5 minutes before they join a simmered dish.
Dried hijiki is soaked 30 minutes in plenty of lukewarm water, then a full hour more in fresh water and washed, which removes the dried-goods smell and debris and restores a plump texture.
Beef is pounded with the back of a knife and chicken or pork is pierced all over with a fork, cutting tough fibers so the meat turns tender and takes in seasoning quickly.
For miso-marinated black cod, the fish is salted and rested 30 minutes on a paper towel, and the moisture that comes out is wiped off before it spends 2 days in the miso marinade.
Green peas for seasoned rice are shelled only just before cooking, because contact with the air makes them hard.

Delicate greens like nanohana are blanched in water held at about 80 degrees Celsius rather than a rolling boil, so their own enzymes keep working to draw out aroma and umami while harsh bitterness stays muted.
Konnyaku is stir-fried in sesame oil for 7 to 8 minutes, until it starts making a chirping sound, because driving its water out first is what lets it drink in seasoning afterward.
Twisting konnyaku through a slit cut in its center, the tezuna style, multiplies its surface area so more of it touches the simmering liquid.
Boiled burdock is pounded flat with the side of a knife before dressing; crushing the fibers lets the seasoning reach the core in a fraction of the usual marinating time.
Asparagus is prepped by snapping off the woody base where it naturally breaks and peeling the lower third of the stalk, and it is cooked whole so its moisture and snap survive.
Cut spring cabbage is soaked in water for about 10 minutes before use, so the leaves drink up moisture and come out crisp and fluffy instead of limp.
For preserved simmered fish, the blood is scrubbed completely out of the belly cavity with chopsticks and paper; any blood left behind turns fishy while the dish keeps.
Salmon pin bones are found by touch, running a fingertip over the flesh, because the bones you can feel are the ones that would ruin a bite.
A cross-hatch cut scored into the skin of a whole grilled fish lets the skin release its tension as it heats, so it does not split or curl and the fish cooks evenly.
Shishito peppers are pierced with a skewer before they are fried, so the steam building inside has an escape route and the peppers do not burst in the oil.
Julienned potatoes are rinsed quickly after cutting to wash off surface starch, which keeps the strands from sticking together and preserves their crisp bite in a stir-fry.
For floury potatoes, the boiled pieces are returned to the dry pot and shaken over the heat until their surfaces turn powdery; that dry, fluffy coating is what makes dressings cling.
Rehydrated hijiki is stir-fried thoroughly in oil until every strand is coated before any simmering liquid is added, which builds richness and keeps the finished dish from tasting watery.
Pork for miso soup is blanched briefly in hot water instead of being stir-fried, so the excess fat leaves with the water and the soup stays clean and light.
Grated onion destined for meatballs is squeezed hard in a cloth first; left wet, it keeps the mixture from binding and dilutes the meat's flavor.
An egg rubbed into chicken as part of its pre-fry marinade keeps the meat from turning tough in the oil, so it fries up plump instead of firm.
Bean sprouts are blanched for only 30 seconds, salted while still hot and left to cool just as they are; rinsing them in water would wash the seasoning back out and turn the dish watery.

practical_steps: Blanch any fish before simmering it: a quick dip in boiling water, then cold water and a gentle wash.
Start root vegetables in a pot of cold water and parboil them about halfway before the main cooking begins.
Re-soak dried seaweed in two changes of water, a short lukewarm soak first and a longer fresh-water soak second.
Salt fish fillets for 30 minutes and wipe off the drawn-out moisture before marinating or grilling.
Pound or fork-pierce meat before marinating when you are short on time, so the flavor reaches the center faster.
Blanch tender spring greens in water that never quite boils, around 80 degrees, for a minute or two, then chill them in cold water.
Squeeze grated onion dry in a cloth before mixing it into any ground-meat mixture.
Fry parboiled konnyaku in a little oil until it chirps before it goes into a simmer, and it will absorb far more flavor.
Pierce small peppers and score fish skin before frying or grilling, so steam and tension have somewhere to go.
scene: A chef's counter an hour before dinner: fish being blanched, root vegetables parboiling from cold water, dried goods swelling in a bowl of water.
theme: In washoku, the cooking is mostly decided before the heat goes on: quiet prep steps remove off-flavors and open the way for seasoning to reach the center.
viewer_takeaways: Most off-flavors can be removed in prep instead of covered up with stronger seasoning.
Cold-water starts and short parboils make vegetables cook evenly and drink in flavor.
A few unhurried prep minutes are the real difference between home cooking and chef cooking.
Touch and sound are prep tools too: bones are found by fingertip, and konnyaku tells you by ear when its water is gone.
